utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that today on the 14th of July, 2005, would I like to greet everyone present, all the representatives of the Prosecution who are in the courtroom today, all the Defence lawyers who are also all present and General Hadzihasanovic and Brigadier Kubura. Naturally I would not wish to forget to mention everyone else present in the courtroom. As you are well aware, we are 20 minutes late because of a technical problem that concerned a faulty cable, so we will not be adjourning at 1.45. We will be adjourning at 2.00 p.m. instead so that no time is lost when the closing arguments are being made. I will now give the floor to General Hadzihasanovic's Defence who will be continuing with their closing argument. I think that Mr. Bourgon has the lectern in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Madam Judge, good day, Mr. President, good day, Your Honour. May it please the Court, it is with pleasure I will continue presenting the closing arguments on behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, and we have been involved in these proceedings for over 18 months as I said yesterday. Mr. President, on your screen you will be able to follow the plan that I will be following when presenting the closing arguments on behalf of General Hadzihasanovic. I'm not quite sure whether the equipment is functioning correctly, but you will see the first issue that I would like to deal with today, and this concerns General Hadzihasanovic as the commander of the 3rd Corps, then I will deal with the applicable law with regard to the responsibility of a commander. This concerns Article 7(3) of the Statute. I will also talk about the lack of a relationship of subordination between the 3rd Corps and the Mujahedin. My colleague will then deal with events mentioned in the indictment. She will commence with counts 1 and 2 and then 5, 6, and 7 will be dealt with. Finally, counts 3 and 4 will be dealt with. Mr. President, this should take us to the last part of our closing argument in which we will deal with the erroneous theories presented by the Prosecution in the course of these proceedings. Naturally, we will also be dealing with preventive measures and -- or present measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic. We will also talk about the current policies of the Tribunal in the light of the charges against General Hadzihasanovic, and finally my colleague will present the Defence's conclusion. Without wasting any more time, Mr. President, I will deal with the first item. Before I do so, there are two minor comments I would like to add. The first one which I forgot to make yesterday was to say my mea culpa to the Trial Chamber given the length of our trial brief. In fact, Mr. President, the trial brief, the final trial brief is longer than it should be according to the practice directive. It is my responsibility. It is my fault because I put the final product together at the very last moment. It is my responsibility alone. I miscalculated the number of pages, and at the very last minute we tried to exclude certain sections, and -- in order to respect the criteria set out in the practice directive. All I can say is that it is my responsibility, Mr. President, and I hope that nevertheless our arguments will be examined as they should be, very carefully, and as I have said, it's my responsibility and the practice directive should be respected. The second issue I'd like to raise concerns criminal law, general criminal law and the principles that should be applied to this trial that we have been involved in for over 18 months, as I have already said on a number of occasions. Criminal law, Mr. President, all lawyers, all criminal lawyers agree that it should be something quite simple, would like it to be quite simple. There are some charges. There is the act that consists of the actus reus and the mens rea. If the Prosecution manages to put the two together and prove beyond all reasonable doubt that these two elements are present, an accused is convicted, and the Trial Chamber has to render a decision on this basis. This law is quite simple, Mr. President, but it requires a rigorous approach, and what we will be presenting you with today are arguments that demonstrate the lack of rigor on the part of the Prosecution's part when presenting its case in this trial. When we're playing with the lives of individuals, with the lives of the accused -- "play" is perhaps not right the term, it's perhaps not the appropriate word, but when we're dealing with criminal law and consequences of what we do will determine whether an individual is a criminal in the eyes of society or not, a criminal who should serve a prison sentence. When we're dealing with such matters, rigor must be demonstrated and the matter must be proved beyond any reasonable doubt. This principle, Mr. President, does not change and must not change because we are before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. On the contrary, this principle must be applied with any greater care. The more serious the consequences, the greater the objective, gravity of an alleged crime is and the more one must be sure that the matter has been proven beyond reasonable doubt if a guilty sentence is delivered. The Chamber mentioned on a number of occasions that the system within which we operate is not a common law system and is not a civil law system either. This is something we understand and something that we accept. It's a unique system that is only in force before this Tribunal. But this clash between these two main judicial systems can give rise to certain difficulties and when there are certain difficulties concerning interpretation. Because of this clash between these two main judicial systems in force in the world, it is our submission, Mr. President, that if there are any doubts as a result of this clash, it should always be to the advantage of the accused. In this system, there is a burden of proof, and the burden of proof is on the Prosecution. It is for the Prosecution to prove its case. And if the Prosecution has failed to prove its case, and this is what we believe, General Hadzihasanovic would then be acquitted on each count in the indictment. Naturally it's not something that will surprise you if I say this in most cases the Prosecution will say, we have acquitted ourselves of a task. We have proven the case beyond any reasonable doubt, and the Defence naturally will tell the Chamber that the Prosecution has not proved its case beyond any reasonable doubt and the accused is not guilty, and this is quite common in all cases. How can one make the same statement and say that in this case it is not just a statement that is being made as a matter of principle, but it is a statement that is of great significance. We believe that the counts in the indictment against General Hadzihasanovic have not been proven. Why is this our opinion? It is our opinion that this is the case because we believe that the Prosecution has failed to understand what is at stake in this case. My colleague said this yesterday, and we wish to reiterate this today. Crimes were committed in Bosnia, without a doubt. There were victims in Central Bosnia. There is no doubt about that. There were victims and crimes that were committed by all the parties in the conflict. There are victims and crimes were committed and there is no doubt about that. It is not because we have a high-ranking commander who is present in the courtroom that we should establish a link between the indictment and the charges, the facts and the victims, the events in question and the victims. This is something that has to be proved. I will now move on to my first item, the performance of General Hadzihasanovic as commander of the 3rd Corps. Who is this person who has been here for 218 sessions? Who is this person sitting in front of you observing you and being observed by you? Who is General Hadzihasanovic. We have heard many witnesses who have had the occasion of meeting General Hadzihasanovic, who have spoken to him, and who have been in a position to assess the type of person he is, individuals who at the time of the events concerned were in a position to see the type of decisions he would take and were in a position to observe the reasons for which he took such decisions. Mr. President, General Hadzihasanovic is not a politician. He has no religious contacts. According to the evidence that has been heard in the course of these proceedings, General Hadzihasanovic is a career officer who first served in the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, and who in spite of everything that we have heard about how officers of Muslim origin were treated in the JNA, in spite of all of the evidence we have heard about this, his talent as a commander and his ability to command was recognised. Reports were drafted in which it was stated that he was an excellent officer. And this is the point of departure that should guide the Chamber when assessing the evidence. General Hadzihasanovic, for reasons that you are well -- that you are familiar with, and these reasons also concern numerous witnesses who have appeared before this Chamber, General Hadzihasanovic left the JNA at a given point in time to join the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Why did he do this? He did this in order to attempt to save his country, Bosnia and Herzegovina. He did not do this for the sake of political or religious principles. He did this in order to save his country that was the subject of aggression committed against it by the VRS. In the course of these proceedings, you have heard that an unofficial attempt was first made to form this army, and subsequently the army was officially formed by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And as we all know, the Presidency took charge of the destiny of the country because they said that there was an imminent threat of war and subsequently there was a state of war that prevailed then. His performance during this period has been commented on by a number of witnesses, and without going over everything that we have included in our final trial brief, it should suffice to mention a few names. For example, General Duncan. Yesterday, I told you what my opinion of General Duncan was. The Chamber witnessed a certain clash between General Duncan and myself in the course of the General's testimony. However, General Duncan is an important person, and what did he say about General Hadzihasanovic? He said that he was an intelligent commander. He said that he was calm. He was a thinker who was in control, a commander who acted and demonstrated diligence when acting. He recognised the fact that he was a commander who had taken necessary and reasonable measures, and he put in place a system of discipline and ensured that these measures were taken. It's slightly improvised translation. In English I'll quote what he said [In English] "He took the necessary and reasonable measures, and he put up a disciplinary system and made sure they happened." [Interpretation] Those are not my words. There is what General Duncan said. Mr. President, General Garrod, Sir Martin Garrod. I still find it difficult to say Sir Martin. He said that General Hadzihasanovic was a good general, an honest general, a general who demonstrated that he was not only capable but that he was also a responsible commander, given his vision of things. What I remember -- what I remember of General Garrod's testimony, well, the Chamber was able to see what sort of a man Martin Garrod was. He said he was a professional soldier in all respects, but he also said General Hadzihasanovic did everything to ensure that his corps functioned and he said he was not a fundamentalist. Witness HI, who was not the last witness, the last person to appear in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he spent a significant time in Bosnia and Herzegovina in a very important position, a position that enabled him to be a privileged witness of everything that took place in Central Bosnia. This is something we have said in our brief. This witness is a witness who, contrary to many others, saw what was happening, realised what was happening, realised what the nature of the game being played by the parties in the conflict was. What did Witness HI say? He said that General Hadzihasanovic wanted a disciplined army, wanted to leave a good impression and took the measures necessary to ensure that that was the case. But the witness added that in fact this was the impression that all the members of his organisation had. He was a career military officer who had all the qualities required to occupy the highest position, that of a corps commander, and to be present in an area that was one of the most important areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that point in time. And he added he was honest, straightforward, and reliable. Mr. President, when the time comes for the Trial Chamber to examine all the evidence, it is our respectful submission that you should bear in mind these comments. If you have any doubts about the significance of such-and-such a document, if you have any doubts about certain games being played by the 3rd Corps in 1993, any duplicity of any kind, well, there were no -- there was no duplicity. All the witnesses have said so. Nothing was concealed. There were no cover-ups, to use the word of my colleague. There was an army in an extremely difficult context, and everyone did their best for the survival of their country, and by doing so they respected all of their legal obligations. So as I have said, there was no hidden agenda. I will move on to this later on. We have referred to the testimony of other witnesses in our brief. Among the international witnesses there was naturally Witness HC, there is witness Bryan Watters, who was the deputy commander of Bob Stewart. I mention this officer because the Prosecution casted doubt on the statement made by Colonel Stewart, on the testimony of Colonel Stewart who appeared here and said, and I'll use his own words, it's a disgrace to see General Hadzihasanovic who has been charged with crimes by this Tribunal. It's not -- the Prosecution said, "Yes, Colonel Stewart, that's not what you said when you testified in the Kordic case," and he said, "Yes, perhaps," but he said nothing bad in the Kordic case. In the Kordic case he quite simply said that the person who had left the best impression on him in Bosnia was Merdan. He said absolutely nothing that would make us doubt the integrity of General Hadzihasanovic. And when he testified before you, he said that this man should not be here before this Tribunal. He said that it was a disgrace. His deputy commander, Bryan Watters, whom you have heard, a Prosecution witness, also said that he was an intelligent commander, an extremely intelligent commander who was capable of adopting an operational vision or strategic vision with regard to the events. He was respected by his men, and he was a military commander who was far better than his counterpart who was Colonel Blaskic. Andrew Jackson, a captain, an officer who worked closely with the 3rd Corps. Jeremy Fleming, a member of the monitoring mission who met the general almost every week. Max Topping who had regular meetings with the general. Lars Baggesen. All these people. Torbjorn Junhov. All of these people are of the same opinion. He is a man of integrity, a good commander and a responsible commander. Naturally one should not forget another witness, a witness from an international organisation. I can't mention the name of the organisation, nor can I mention the name of the person in question. But this person said, and this person expressed a different point of view. This person was not examining the accomplishment of the mission or commenting on the accomplishment of the general's mission which is what we are concerned with, but this person had one thing in mind, that was the harmony among people, the passage of humanitarian convoys, the survival of the population. And what did this witness say about General Hadzihasanovic? The witness said General Hadzihasanovic said that he was making efforts to protect the population, to protect the Croatian population in Zenica and in the surrounding villages. The witness added in practice these efforts were made. And General Hadzihasanovic did everything that was necessary to ensure that humanitarian convoys could pass through. There are also local witnesses, Mr. President, and as far as these witnesses are concerned, all I will do is mention witnesses who were not members of the 3rd Corps. For example, a witness such as Veseljak. He talked about measures implemented by General Hadzihasanovic. Witnesses who testified before this Chamber, and some of them by way of example are Serbs. We did have Serbs who testified here, Serbs from Zenica. What did they say about General Hadzihasanovic? What were these Serbs doing in Zenica in 1993? Why did they stay there? Because they realised that efforts were being made in order to make it possible for the Croat population to stay in Zenica. And opposed to what the Prosecution has said when they cast doubt on the sincerity of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in terms of promoting a multi-ethnic society. We've said it in our brief, Mr. President. You only need to compare the manifesto of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the same level documents coming either from the Republika Srpska or from the HVO. And you can see the difference straight away. You can see that the HVO and the VRS have territorial expansionist ambitions, and you can see that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopts a responsible approach in order to protect their territory and their country on the basis of a multi-ethnic approach And from our point of view, General Hadzihasanovic was in agreement with this policy, and that was his guiding principle, in all of his duties and all of his tasks, everything that he accomplished in 1993. A little bit later I'm going to refer to measures spoken of by witnesses who came here and told us things had changes when General Hadzihasanovic arrived. He introduced some order. He did not go along with the 3rd Corps policy. That was quite obvious. Had there been any crimes? Yes, Mr. President. And had there been any pillaging? Yes. Had houses been looted? Yes, Mr. President, houses had been looted. But we still need to establish link between the looted houses and the commander of an army corps who commands more than 30.000 men. But not 30.000 men that are like players in a chess game. He needs to organise and kind of task that would require at least 40.000 people in order to just hold the front line, and this is something that has not been argued against in the report of our expert witness Karavelic. Simply holding the front line would have required 40.000 men, just for the front line. If you look at the annexes to the witness -- expert witness report, you can see that there is a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you can see all the dotted lines on top of that map, and those dotted lines indicate the areas of responsibility of each individual brigade, and you can see that they go all the way around the map. Unfortunately in the course of your visit in Bosnia, I don't know, but apparently on the basis of the report that I've read you are supposed to have seen the front line, but it is very difficult to go out in the field and try and imagine a front line which is about 400 or 300 kilometres long. It is extremely difficult. I mean, I spent quite a few years in the army myself, and I visited Bosnia with General Polutak, and he explained to me about these front lines and he indicated where they were, but I just could not picture them. I could not imagine them. I found it very difficult to create a clear image of the front line in my mind. It is very difficult to understand, and so we have to trust those witnesses who were there at the time. And General Karavelic said that 40.000 people would be needed simply to hold the front line, and there were approximately 30.000, a little bit less, a little bit more. So this means that there were no reserve forces. It doesn't really matter what the legal of a commander is, and this is what we've talked about with General Reinhardt, and that's his area of expertise, commanding troops, and we've talked about him -- about it with him in the course of the cross-examination. What does it mean for a commander not to have any reserve forces? A commander who does not have any reserve forces is a commander who has no freedom of action. He can only react. He can be reactive but not pro-active. He is no longer able to think ahead, to command. In this case, General Hadzihasanovic had to juggle the forces that he had available at all times, and he basically had to make decisions, "Shall I sacrifice this bit of the front line to the advantage of such-and-such a secondary operation?" And that was the challenge he had to face up to on a daily basis. What he tried to do, what he managed to do was to command his army corps whilst trying to respect his legal obligations as much as possible. Let me now move on to the second point of my presentation this morning, that is to say Article 7(3) of the Statute. This article, Article 7(3) is referred to on page 16 of our final brief -- or, rather, of the Prosecution's brief, and we did it as well on pages 196 to 200. It is also interesting to mention that the Chamber had already dealt with this with regard to Mr. Hadzihasanovic's Defence according to Article 98 bis of the regulation. We fully agree with the point of view of the Trial Chamber on this topic. So my point today, my aim today, is to first of all explain that certain things impose themselves to suggest to the Trial Chamber what in our view is the best way of interpreting and using Article 7(3) of the Statute in this case. This article deals only and exclusively with the responsibilities of a commander. I believe, Mr. President, that I can't even count the number of times I've mentioned this, and I don't think I'll ever mention it often enough, because it is for that reason that we are here. The provisions of the Article 7(3) of the Statute, in order to establish whether a commander has carried out his duties properly, or whether he's a criminal, he acted in such a way which would mean that he has to go to prison, that's why we're here. But General Hadzihasanovic is, in our view, absolutely not the type of general who failed to act in line with his duties with regard to every single count of the indictment, and we really don't see that he should be sentenced to a prison sentence. You're not facing a criminal here. You're facing a commander who has exercised the highest possible duties in one of the most difficulty contexts imaginable. We can ask what is -- anyone can ask what is the most difficult moment in a person's life. Your Honours, what is the most difficult, what has been the most difficult moment in your lives? Difficult either professionally speaking or on a purely human level, as a human being. And when I asked myself that question I found it very difficult to come up with an answer. Professionally speaking, for example, it was when I represented a client who was a Albanian from Kosovo, and I had to make extremely difficult decisions on his behalf because he claimed that he was not the right person, he was not the person who should have been brought before this Court. And it was an extremely difficult time for me from a purely professional point of view since it entailed serious consequences for that person. That was the most difficult professional moment for me. Your Honours, my colleagues, anyone in this room can probably think of such a moment in their professional lives. But what I'm trying to say, Mr. President, and I don't think I'm wrong, obviously I can't make sure but I believe the context in which General Hadzihasanovic had to work and to carry out his duties in 1993 goes far beyond anything that any of us in this room can even imagine in terms of our professional duties, in our professional lives and careers. Obviously, Mr. President, I'm making this comment with all due respect, because of course I have no intimate knowledge of other people's professional lives, especially Your Honours, but it is just a comparison in order to illustrate the extremely difficult context in which General Hadzihasanovic had to work. So Article 7(3) of the Statute, which deals with the responsibilities of a commander, let me just make another statement. If somebody is accused, because Article 7(2) and 7(3), together or if you have simply 7(3) -- well, there is a big difference between the two. There is a fundamental difference because on both sides there may be the presumption of innocence, but on the other hand there are actual allegations of actual participation of the person involved in those crimes, whereas on the other hand the allegations have to do with a failure to carry out his duties as a commander. But this is a totally different situation, and it is very difficult when we need to establish the mens rea, did they have -- did they know or have reason to know or -- and consequently did they act and implement reasonable and necessary measures. As the deposition adopted by the Prosecution -- I'm speeding up here a little bit because I see the clock is ticking. The Prosecution made their point by giving us a selection of various statements that they appreciated and that they found in 16 different decisions or, rather, 11 decisions of the Chamber of first instance and 16 of the Appeals Chamber with regard to Article 7(3). Any statement that they like they just put together. They pasted them together and they presented them to you. We, on our part, have not done that. Why? Because we have made an attempt to give you a point of view which would reflect both the case law before the International Tribunal in its entirety but which would also be consistent from the beginning to the end with the application of the provisions of Article 7(3). What is the last sentence passed with regard to that Article? It is case Strugar and the sentence was passed in the month of January, 2005. The accused, Strugar, was faced with acquisitions with regard to 7(1) and 7(3), but he was only recognised guilty on the basis of Article 7(3). And I believe that this is where we have -- we can compare the two cases. I mean, we all agree on the three basic elements in 7(3); that is to say, the existence of a subordination link, the knowledge on the part of the accused; that is to say, we must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused knew or had reason to know, and finally failure to act on the part of the accused; that is to say, it must be proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused failed to implement the necessary measures in order to prevent such crimes being committed or to punish the perpetrators. There are no major differences of opinion between the two parties on this level. The differences do arise when this comes to the actual implementation and application of these three criteria. The decisive criterion concerning the existence of a link of subordination between the accused and the perpetrators of a crime is the actual effective control being exercised by the commander over his men. On this point we do agree with the Trial Chamber. We are also of the view that this control may be a control de jure or a control de facto. We've already explained this in our final brief. It goes without saying following a decision of the Appeals Chamber in this very case that that control must be exercised by the commander on the very time when those crimes are about to be committed or have been committed. Where we do have a difference of opinions is the interpretation of this term "effective control." In our view it is quite clear and unambiguous. There has to be control and that control must be effective. What does that mean in practice? First of all, the Appeals Chamber recognised the need to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that the perpetrator of a crime was subordinated to the accused. The Appeals Chamber added in the Blaskic ruling that this is more a matter of proving facts rather than a matter of law, of the legal situation. According to the Appeals Chamber, it must be proven beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused had the authority to prevent, punish, or introduce measures leading to procedures to be implemented with regard to the perpetrators. Such authority must be a real authority and in practice and not just a theoretical one. It is simply not sufficient, Mr. President, for a commander to be a commander on paper; in other words, to have this de jure authority. We still need to prove that the commander did indeed exercise this effective control in practice. What does it mean to exercise actual control in practice? Our reply to this question is that a commander has the authority to prevent when he has the material possibility to issue orders to those subordinated to him, a group of people or an individual, and that those individuals have to carry out those orders, and unless they do they would be liable to incur disciplinary measures or even face criminal proceedings. So there is this actual authority when orders can be issued in full knowledge that the people he's issuing the orders to must carry them out. This was explained by General Sir Martin Garrod in a very succinct manner but a precise manner as well. The Chamber asked him a question: "In your capacity as a high-level officer, what do you think that this motion means?" He replied, and I quote: [In English] The elements of the forces in your area were carrying out your orders and that you knew exactly what they were doing and they were not doing anything that was unacceptable to you." [Interpretation] This was an off-the-cuff answer from a high-ranking general. Now, the point in which General Garrod did not have -- tended to elaborate very much is the following: Why do the forces carry out orders, and why does he know what his forces do? I mean, how did this come about in a real-life situation? Now, the reply is very simple, in fact. The first possibility, the forces in question, the troops subordinated to a general must carry out orders, and they also must inform the commander in the course of any controls of their -- of whatever has been done. The second possibility, because they accept the idea that the commander has control over them. And in both cases, Mr. President, the forces in question carrying out those orders, because they feel that it is their duty and their obligation to do that or because they accept to carry out orders, in both cases, Mr. President, those troops are fully aware of the fact that unless they do carry out those orders they would be liable to incur certain measures which might be imposed by the commander. And this leads us to the next question; that is to say, what does it mean to have the material, the actual possibility to impose measures about those subordinated to a commander? The Appeals Chamber answered that question as well by saying it means to implement the necessary measures in order to ensure that the perpetrators of a crime will have to -- will be held accountable for their actions before a court of justice. In the Strugar case, the accused was a commander of the 2nd Operational Group. It is not the same sort of operational group that we've heard about in the course of this case. I believe that in as far as the Serb army was concerned, the operational group was considered to be at a somewhat higher level. The units responsible for crimes in this case, we're talking about the attacks and the legal shelling of the old town of Dubrovnik, and it was the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade. At first site that battalion was part of a brigade which was a part of an operational group over which the accused Strugar had command. The Trial Chamber proceeded to carry out a detailed analysis, first of all, of the actual command structure, the existing command structure. Secondly, of the authority of the accused, the authority that he had in order to prevent the legal shelling of the old town of Dubrovnik. And thirdly, the material possibility that he had to punish the perpetrators of such illegal shelling. It was a lengthy exercise on the part of the Chamber of first instance, and the conclusion was reached that the legal authority was there and that the accused also had the material possibility to issue orders to the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade, in order to prevent this attack as well as to implement other measures to ensure that that order was acted upon, or that if the town had been shelled, he also had the authority to issue orders in order for that attack to stop. The Chamber declared itself satisfied that the accused had the legal authority and the material possibility to start an inquiry and to impose disciplinary, administrative measures against officers responsible for that shelling. We respectfully submit to you, Mr. President, that this is the same sort of exercise that this Trial Chamber could perhaps carry out in this case in order to determine whether there was indeed a link of subordination between General Hadzihasanovic and those notorious Mujahedin. We still don't know who they are, but at any rate, the Mujahedin who are supposed to have carried out the crimes referred to in the indictment. We are confident that the Chamber will recognise that at no time in the course of 1993 General Hadzihasanovic had such control over such individuals no matter who they were. Let me take this opportunity to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case. This is something which has already been referred to in what we said with regard to Article 98 bis. We are talking about the 98 bis motion. We had General Blaskic who had the material possibility to issue orders to the 4th Battalion of the military police. The 4th Battalion of the military police was a unit which was a part - I do apologise - a part of the HVO group in its BOZ in Central Bosnia. The Operational Zone called Central Bosnia. I do apologise, Mr. President. So at any rate, they were a part of that, of the formations under Colonel Blaskic's command. He did, in fact, issue a number of orders to the military police battalion, and in fact, that battalion did carry out quite a few of those orders. Orders were being issued and were being acted upon. And we're talking about the communication between Colonel Blaskic and the 4th Military Police Battalion. However, in its assessment in order to establish whether there was such a link of subordination between Colonel Blaskic and the military police battalion at the time of the attack on Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, the Appeals Chamber said no, Colonel Blaskic did not at that particular moment exercise effective control over such units. If we look at that example and take it as our point of departure, and if we look at the analysis carry out by the first -- by the Chamber of first instance in the Blaskic case, and if we try and apply this to those notorious Mujahedin, well, Mr. Chairman -- Mr. President, we really don't see how we can reach a conclusion on the basis of a number of documents or examples where Mujahedin was found in someplace or the commander heard about the death of three Mujahedin following combat activity. We really don't see how the elements of proof provided by the Prosecution so far could lead you to establish such a link and to find that such a link of subordination did indeed exist between General Hadzihasanovic and the Mujahedin. And with regard to the second element, knowledge, it must be proven beyond any reasonable doubt, and we've stressed it once again in our final brief, that the accused knew or had reason to know. Let us draw the Chamber's attention once again to the fact that Article 7(3) does not introduce a form of absolute responsibility here or a form of responsibility strictly speaking. The second element must be separated in two parts: Did the accused know, or did he have reason to know? As to whether he knew, that is to say this is something that can be established on the basis of a direct proof, but the Prosecution did indeed say they did not have such proof, or we could have circumstantial evidence. What is more important is to see how can we properly interpret the expression "had reason to know." The Appeals Chamber clearly established that a commander would know -- not know it unless specific information had actually been in his possession and that that information was of such nature as to lead the commander to conclude that an infringement or a crime had been committed or was about to be committed by his subordinates and that it was his duty to start an inquiry. When arguing on the basis of Article 7(3), the Prosecution elaborated at length on the issue of risk. There is a distinction between the Prosecution and the Defence as far as this is concerned. The Prosecution says that risk in itself is sufficient to arrive at the conclusion that a commander had reason to know. We do not accept such a broad interpretation that would be synonymous to absolute -- synonymous with absolute responsibility or responsibility in the strict sense of the term. There's always the risk that one's subordinates will commit crimes. That's more than just a risk. In our opinion, the idea of risk can perhaps be applied in the case of Article 7(1) of the Statute. In that case, mens rea can be established on the basis of the doctrine dolus eventualis. The Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case decided that an accused could have the -- have acquired mens rea given the violation of having ordered that a crime be committed, but when an attack is being ordered, there has to be a significant possibility or a substantial likelihood that a violation will be committed when the order issued is being carried out. This is why there was a huge difference in the final decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case and the Trial Chamber's decision. As a result, Mr. President, if the evidence has to prove that there is a significant risk that a violation might be committed, this is the dolus eventualis for the Prosecution pursuant to 7(1) of the article, it is our opinion that the simple risk that a violation may be committed is not sufficient to arrive at the conclusion that a commander had reason to know pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute. The Trial Chamber in the Strugar case reached the same conclusion. In legal terms, the Trial Chamber confirmed that a commander will incur criminal liability only if specific information was really available to him and this information allowed him to come to the conclusion that violations had been committed by a subordinate. This is the decision of the Appeals Chamber. But they Strugar had to apply these criteria to a specific situation. First of all, they set aside the notion of risk, the possibility of risk or to use the English expression, the idea that a violation might be committed. They said no. When we simply read through Article 7(3), this eliminates the idea that a violation might be committed. Nevertheless, the Chamber also dismissed the idea of certainty. They said, "We cannot interpret Article 7(3) in the following way: We can't say that a commander has to be certain that a crime was committed or might be committed before he can take measures." So the two extremes were dismissed, the risk that has been suggested by the Prosecution and certainty that would -- the idea of certainty that would go against Article 7(3). As a result, the Trial Chamber came to the conclusion that information available to the commander must allow the commander to come to the conclusion that there is a real possibility of a violation being committed. Once again, this is my translation. I believe that the English term is "a clear prospect." And this is the result the Chamber arrived at. The town of Dubrovnik was illegally shelled in October 1991. The town of Dubrovnik was shelled illegally again in November of 1991. So first there was the illegal shelling of Dubrovnik in October and then in November. No one was prosecuted for these two criminal acts. On the 6th of December orders were issued by the accused Strugar to order an attack on the town of Srd, S-r-d, which is in the vicinity of the old town of Dubrovnik. The Chamber reached the conclusion that there was the real possibility that in the course of the shelling the same troops that had illegally shelled the town in October and November might engage in the illegal shelling of the old town of Dubrovnik. In spite of these conclusions, the Chamber decided that this was not sufficient to say that the accused had reason to know. In our opinion, this is an important example, one which we support. In the same case, according to the facts, the accused refused information or dismissed information in the course of the day according to which the town was being shelled on the 6th of December. And this was at the time when this attack on Srd that had been ordered by Strugar was taking place. The Chamber concluded that the line had just been crossed at that point in time. Even if one did not know who was shelling the old town, at that point in time he had sufficient information to say, "I should carry out investigations to make sure that these are not my subordinates who are attacking the town of Dubrovnik." At that point in time, the line had been crossed and he had reason to know. So it was his duty to carry out investigations. This example suffices to demonstrate the level and nature of information that a commander has to have in order to have reason to know. The third criteria -- the third criterion, Mr. President, taking reasonable measures to ensure that subordinates do not commit crimes, is a criterion I will deal with when I deal with the issue of the measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic. I don't want to repeat all of the details that are contained in our final trial brief. However, there is one subject I would like to address before the Chamber. When my colleague dealings with the charges levelled against the General, the subject is, the issue is that the position of an individual in the hierarchy is very important because it is on this position that the nature of measures taken depends. According to the case law, the type of measures that can be taken include reports on activities of units including issuing orders to prevent violations from being committed include issuing orders to ensure that violations ended, include protests against violations, include disciplinary measures. This also involves insisting, emphasising to one superior's that measures should be taken. One must also ensure that one's subordinates know what their obligations are. Mr. President, as far as this is concerned, I would simply like to remind you of what General Cordy-Simpson said before you. The following question was put to him: "General, I would like to know whether you can see any difference between the responsibility of a battalion commander and the responsibility of a corps commander with regard to their men and to what extent does a commander have to be personally involved in the matter?" I don't want to mistranslate this. I'll quote General Cordy-Simpson's answer in English: "[In English] It is my belief that battalion command is the last time an officer will directly influence how his soldiers perform on the battlefield. He is responsible. He is the man they see. He can will them to fight better than any other person in the battalion. "Once you become a brigade commander or a divisional commander or a corps commander, that direct influence is lost. As a brigade commander, you would tell your battalion commanders what you require them to do, but you cannot permanently influence the individual soldiers within that battalion to fight harder, fight better, or anything else. Certainly when you become a divisional commander, you have totally lost the ability to influence the battle of how people fight, and as a corps commander you are way above that. You are directing the battle at the high tactical, I would put it, level, but you are not directly influencing how soldiers fight on the ground at that particular moment." [Interpretation] And the following question: "... what should a corps commander do to prevent violations from happening, bearing in mind what you just said as to what he can and cannot do?"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: He can only lay down to his battalion commanders, or in the case of a corps commander to his divisional commanders and his brigade commanders, how he wishes operations to be conducted and on what sort of code of behaviour. Having passed that information, he must either expect that his subordinates will carry out his orders, or if he finds subsequent that they haven't carried out his orders, then he must order an investigation into why that has not happened. But he cannot influence the individual actions of soldiers on the ground at a particular moment in time." [Interpretation] This testimony given by General Cordy-Simpson, if we examine it in the light of paragraph 375 of the Trial Chamber's decision in the Strugar case, and they quote paragraph 3.560 and 3.561 in this regard, the comments on the first additional protocol to the Geneva Conventions, then we immediately see that the measures in question are different depending on the level and position of a commander. I'll stop here, Mr. President. I think that it is time for a break now, and after the break I will immediately address factual issues that concern the lack of relationship of subordination between General Hadzihasanovic or the 3rd Corps of the ABiH and the so-called Mujahedin. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have our break now, and we will resume not at 11.00 but at ten to 11.00 in order to try and make up for the time that we lost at the beginning of the session. So we will resume at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May it please the Court. Mr. President, Madam Judge, Your Honour, I will now deal with the absence of a relationship of subordination between the Mujahedin and the 3rd Corps. The time has come, Mr. President, to distinguish between fiction and reality, to make a distinction between the fabrications of the Prosecution and the actual situation such as it was experienced by General Hadzihasanovic in the field in 1993. Mr. President, what is most surprising at this stage is that in the course of presenting its closing arguments the Prosecution failed to present a coherent theory which would establish this supposed relationship of subordination between the 3rd Corps and the Mujahedin. On the one hand since Monday the Prosecution has a new battle horse, namely the joint combat operations between the Mujahedin and the ABiH in 1992 and 1993. On the other hand, and this is more interesting, there is the approach of my colleague who presented the arguments for the Prosecution with regard to the first count that concerns the events in Dusina, Miletici and Maline. My colleague from the Prosecution then demonstrated what the Prosecution's actual theory was, and I quote in English: [In English] "I don't want to go over it. The Mujahedins are all over. They are acknowledged. They are taken into account. They will are a factor. They acknowledge that they were there, and they had influence to the very least over these Mujahedin and could change their behaviour." [Interpretation] 12th of July, transcript page 52 to 53. Mr. President, this is the Prosecution's real position. The Mujahedin were there. The army knew that the Mujahedin were there. The army at any point of time could have exercised or could have influenced them in order to make them change their behaviour. There is no doubt that we are light years away from establishing effective -- the existence of effective control over the Mujahedin in accordance with the criteria that have been recognised by the case law of the International Tribunal. The Defence has presented you with a lot of evidence that demonstrates that the commander of the 3rd Corps had absolutely no influence over the Mujahedin. The Mujahedin didn't want -- wanted nothing to do with General Hadzihasanovic. The evidence shows that there was a real desire to solve the problem. A first comment should be made before I deal with the evidence in the case. In order to establish a relationship of subordination between the 3rd Corps and the so-called Mujahedin, Mr. President, it is necessary to assess the evidence in the light of the applicable law in relation to effective control such as it has already been elaborated. Our position is very clear and contrary to the Prosecution position, our position has not changed. In 1993, there was no relationship of subordination pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute between the 3rd Corps and the Mujahedin. On the other hand, what has been quite clearly established, this is something I have already mentioned, is the fact that the 3rd Corps commanders as well as the leaders of the ABiH realised the sort of problem caused by the presence of the so-called Mujahedin, and throughout 1993, they tried to solve the problem on a number of occasions and in a number of ways. However, they failed to do so. We are aware of the fact, and the evidence demonstrates this fact. It's necessary to make another comment at this point. Mr. President, it is essential to assess the evidence with regard to the so-called Mujahedin in the light of the situation that prevailed in 1993 and not in the light of everything that has come to light, everything that the international community has discovered with regard to terrorism and al Qaeda and with regard to the Mujahedin in the year 2005. In 1993, when these foreigners appeared in Central Bosnia, the Bosniaks soon noticed that they were different, but initially they were not perceived as being a possible source of crime. A number of witnesses have said that the term "Mujahedin" or "holy warrior" was a term they were not familiar with at the time. So it is through the eyes of Bosniaks in 1993 that one should assess the situation. Today we are more familiar with the phenomenon of terrorism and with the phenomenon of the Mujahedin. We are well aware of what happened in London a few days ago. We are all aware of the existence of al Qaeda throughout the world. We are aware of the events in New York. We are aware of the war in Iraq. We know that things took place in Afghanistan. We are familiar with Mujahedin being held at the American base in Cuba. We are all aware of this, and we see Mujahedin every day with explosives stopped to their bodies. We are aware of these individuals who blow themselves up for reasons unknown to us. We are familiar with these cases of violence, and it is certain today that if the same Mujahedin arrived in Bosnia today, the Bosniaks would react differently, but this was not knowledge available to them at the time, not in 1992 and 1993. It is our respectful submission, Mr. President, that had it not been for the foresight of General Hadzihasanovic in 1993, General Hadzihasanovic had realised what the problem was and tried to find a solution without compromising his mission. It is our submission that if it had not been for such foresight, the results of the conflict could have been catastrophic. I'm not referring necessarily to the conflict involving the Mujahedin. I'm referring to the conflict in Central Bosnia. As far as the Prosecution's theory on the so-called Mujahedin is concerned, there is a second point I would like to make. Having investigated, having carried out investigations for over five years and in spite of the fact that the Prosecution decided that the Mujahedin should be a priority target in their investigations, and this has been confirmed by the investigator, in spite of this fact the Prosecution has not managed to establish the existence of a relationship of subordination between the 3rd Corps and the so-called Mujahedin pursuant to the provisions of Article 7(3). Now, Mr. President, I'll return to this subject a little later, but it is quite clear for us that had it not been for the existence of these notorious Mujahedin, General Hadzihasanovic would not be here today because he would not have been indicted by this Tribunal. It appears quite clear to us that the Prosecution has tried to use General Hadzihasanovic in order to punish the crimes committed by the so-called Mujahedin in Central Bosnia in 1993. And the Prosecution's new battle horse relates to joint combat operations. Mr. President, one should note from the outset that a joint combat operation does not entail necessarily a relationship of subordination between the participants in such an operation. On the other hand, or to the contrary, joint combat operation involves planning, organisation, issuing orders, precise orders, in order to avoid incidents occurring when two forces are involved in joint action. Mr. President, if there is -- if there are joint operations, this involves the presence of individuals who have not been invited. They're acting independently in the course of a planned action. The Defence's military expert said in the course of his testimony that there were certain risks involved if individuals appeared and participated in an attack without this having been planned, without this having been expected. This relates to the notion of joint combat operations. That proved that the appearance of the Mujahedin in the course of such combat was planned and perhaps there was joint action at that point in time. To do this it is necessary to provide evidence relating to the planning of the combat action, the organisation of the combat action. But in this case, the Prosecution have provided a number of examples to us in which the Mujahedin or the Arabs or Turks whose identity and origin we are unaware of were observed in the course of combat operations or in other circumstances. But they have not presented any evidence that would show that there was planning, preparation, organisation of such action. One of the examples used by the Prosecution concerns Witness HF, a Defence witness who mentioned the presence of the Mujahedin at the front line in Bijela Buca. This witness said: "[In English] They would go there on their own initiative and carry out some operations that were more disadvantaged to us than any real use, because they would only provoke artillery fire. [Interpretation] The Prosecution can say as many times as they like that they don't believe that witness. It's not useful for as long as they don't have any proof to the contrary. So in conclusion, there has not even been any joint combat activity. And even if there had been such a joint combat activity, it was not done under an effective control of the commander here. As to combat operations in April 1993 in the area of Zmajevac, we have three sources of information with regard to this evidence, but in the light of the actual analysis of those documents and in the light of the statement made by the witness on behalf of the co-accused, it is simply not possible, Mr. President, to conclude that there had indeed been some joint combat activity with Arabs, Turks, or the Mujahedin. And even less so as to the existence of effective control of the 3rd Corps over those individuals. As to taking of arms in Mravinjac in the second half of June, we had three sources of information there, and it is indicated that the 3rd Battalion of the 17th Brigade, Mountain Brigade called Krajina, got a tank and a number of weapons in B790. It is about the seizing of combat or assault tank and armaments and -- by three brigades, 307th, 308th, 17th, and the 7th. And this is mentioned by the commander of the Operational Group Zapad. Finally, we have two contradictory references in P798 -- P598, sorry. Arabs apparently captured an assault tank at Mravinac, and further on in the same document there was a reference to people from Novi Travnik who were supposed to have seized such a tank and some more weapons at Mravinac. On the basis of those documents, it is simply not possible to conclude that there was indeed some joint combat activity and even less so that there was an existence of effective control on the part of the 3rd Corps of Arabs, Turks, or the Mujahedin. On top of that it is also important to analyse document P598 in the light of the conclusion drawn by the Witness ZP with regard to Ramo Abu Dzihad. As to the activities of the 333rd Brigade, between the 10th and the 14th of July, 1993, and we've got the documentary evidence P434, P924 part 4, which is part of the C section, I believe, then P603, P605, and C16. The Trial Chamber heard from General Merdan on this topic, and he provided his own explanations. In the light of the witness statement on the part of Merdan and on the basis of our analysis of all the possible correlations between these documents, we are of the view that it is not possible to conclude that there was any joint combat activity, and especially that there was some kind of effective control on the part of the 3rd Corps over the Arabs or the unknown unit which is referred to in one of those documents. Since we are indeed talking about an unknown unit, it is quite significant in this context to mention that the 333rd Brigade had never participate -- participated in any operation required by 3rd Corps with regard to the contents of the document P603. So the suggestion is quite simple. The 3rd Corps said no, and then this unit that we don't know what it is, it is not a unit which is within the framework of our army, and they said, "We can't issue orders to them because it is not within the framework of the BH army." If this unit were to be included, it would have to be referred to in the combat report. And if you look at the combat reports of the 333rd Brigade and all the documents of the 333rd Brigade following that period, there is no reference whatsoever to the use of this unknown unit. We also respectfully submit that this unknown unit might be something totally different from the Arabs referred to in another document. With regard to P477, which is a report drawn up by General Hadzihasanovic mentioning the fact that the Mujahedin had refused to participate in the combat activity, it is a document or an event which took place just before the order from the high command aimed at setting up an El Mujahid unit. It doesn't really matter for what reason the Mujahedin refused to participate in combat activity. It goes to show very clearly that there was a clear lack of control over those elements whose identity - and let me just remind you of this - is still unknown. Our viewpoint on this has not changed. It was a part of the approach undertaken with the aim to solve the Mujahedin problem. As we know in the light of all evidence, this approach actually failed. Now, this conclusion leads us to the period of time between the 3rd of August, 1993, the date when the order was issued to set up the El Mujahedin unit until September 1993, and the actual evidence does not allow us to establish with any degree of precision what exact approaches and activities had been undertaken in order to carry out the order which was issued on the 13th of August. Where do the members of the El Mujahid come from? We still don't know. Where do the locals who are supposed to have joined El Mujahid come from? We still don't know. Have any orders been issued in order to appoint the commander and the deputy commander of El Mujahid? No documents on this. And we do know the appointment of a commander must go through the high command. Had any documents been issued concerning the organisation, the equipment, the make-up, the geographical area of this El Mujahid unit, there again we have no documents whatsoever in this respect. The Prosecution claims that Alagic had witnessed the setting up of El Mujahid on the basis of one of the propaganda videos obtained from an unknown source representing an unknown place on an unknown day. This evidence does not allow us to draw such a conclusion. Where is the command and General Staff of El Mujahid at Podbrezje, at Orasac, Arnauti, Zenica, Poljanice? No idea, Mr. President. According to Witness HF, the presence of Mujahedin has been recorded, is supposed to have been recorded in those places at different points in time. How many Mujahedin are there? How many had there been in Central Bosnia? What is the total number, and where were they? We don't know. How many locals wearing such clothes were there in those areas? We still don't know. What we do know, though, is the fact that there had been attempts made at placing them under the control of 306th Brigade, but it did not work. My colleague supplied the information in this regard here. The 3rd Corps also tried to place El Mujahid under the operational control, the operational group at Grabica, and we know what happened afterwards. That is to say under the operational control of OGBK, and we know what happened afterwards. And especially combat activity was organised by the 17th KBBR, and Commander Cuskic talked about this activity of having an operation with the El Mujahid. And he talked about implications of engaging in an operation with the Mujahedin, and he said to what extent such combat activity has led to disastrous results and that, as far as he was concerned, he never ever wanted to repeat the experience. Afterwards, no other similar activity had been either planned or organised, at least not until the date at which General Hadzihasanovic left his post as commander of the 3rd Corps on the 1st of November, 1993. Finally, as is explained in our brief, we do know that an large-scale operation was carried out in order to dismantle the Turkish guerrilla under the command of Kemal. We also refer to the witness statements of Muratovic and Witness HD. And we also know that even in February 1994, this matter of Mujahedin still had not been solved. By way of conclusion as to the joint combat activities alleged by the Prosecution, I would like to also take this opportunity to refer to the use of Mujahedin in terms of them heading combat activity. Our position in this respect is quite clear. No Mujahedin were used in order to spearhead any combat activity of the 3rd Corps. This is with regard to the witness statement by General Reinhardt, and he was talking about a topic on which he had a certain amount of expertise. General Reinhardt confirmed that the use of such combat unit as -- in this respect would require the maximum level of coordination. Now, it is obvious in the light of the evidence we've got that there had never been such a coordination or such planning or organisation between the 3rd Corps and the Arabs, Turks, or the Mujahedin. What did Major Bower have to say about this? The answer is quite simple. The conclusion that he's reached on this topic, and that is the statement used by the Prosecution, well, it concerned the 7th Brigade. He simply confused the 7th Brigade and the Mujahedin. If we re-read this quote, we can see that references to the 7th Brigade. He's not talking about this brigade committing atrocities. He was talking about a brigade engaged in combat activity which was there where the activity was most intense. That brigade had participated, was one of the mobile brigades, as many other brigades of the 3rd Corps. He saw that brigade and he simply confused that brigade with the existence of the Mujahedin, and this is an altogether different matter. Without trying to go through the details of all the international witnesses once again, but especially with regard to what the Prosecution has said in order to support their assumptions, but it is quite clear that they had nothing to base their impressions on, no concrete, tangible, practical facts that had been observed by these witnesses. The Prosecution seems to have forgotten a key witness when it comes to the absence of the link of subordination between the Mujahedin and the 3rd Corps. The witness HI was a privileged witness with regard to all the events taking place in Central Bosnia up until the month of September 1993. As we do know, this witness was everywhere at that time. And what was his conclusion with regard to the Mujahedin? He said, "In the course of my mandate in Central Bosnia, there was no indication whatsoever that foreign combatants or fighters or Mujahedin were subordinated to the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there was no indication whatsoever that they were cooperating with them." In their closing brief, the Prosecution refers to additional indications which in their view should lead us to conclude that the Mujahedin were indeed an integral part of the 3rd Corps units. According to the Prosecution, the Mujahedin are supposed to have trained members and units of the 3rd Corps or would have supplied some logistical support to them. As to any logistical support that is supposed to have been supplied, the Prosecution has provided no evidence to support that claim. The evidence tends to suggest the contrary, rather. As we had pointed out, the Mujahedin had never provided any logistical support, and the 3rd Corps could not supply the Mujahedin with any logistical support either. The evidence suggests furthermore that the Mujahedin had never trained any members of the 3rd Corps. The witnesses Jasarevic, Husic, Siljak, Jusufspahic, and the witness HB, Caber confirmed that members of the 3rd Corps had not been trained by the Mujahedin. The Prosecution confers -- refers to the bad treatment that the Mujahedin had been subjected to. Quite interestingly, in paragraphs 156 to 159 of their brief, the Prosecution claims that there had been complaints lodged to the HVO with regard to the detention of foreign citizens and that that makes it possible to conclude that between February and the 12th of April, 1993, at least 24 Mujahedin members of the 7th Brigade would have been captured or arrested by the HVO. Those documents, Mr. President, do not, quite simply, allow us to draw such a conclusion. It is simply impossible in the light of this document to conclude that those foreigners who were apprehended or arrested were members of any unit at all of the 3rd Corps. Had the General Hadzihasanovic wanted to lodge a complaint with Colonel Blaskic with regard to the arrests and the illegal detention of his subordinates, members of the 3rd Corps, he would certainly not have envisaged any diplomatic channels through which to do it. The implication of the Mujahedin in the kidnapping of Totic, we've been able to demonstrate this in the course of the trial that they were not at all involved in the kidnapping of Totic and even less so with regard to his military police battalion. The reference is to Witness HD, Witness HF, Witness Saric, ZP, Mahir, Ibrakovic, as well as Witness HI who was an international witness. The 3rd Corps, more specifically Merdan, had never been involved in any negotiations between the Mujahedin, the European Community Monitoring Mission and the HVO, and especially we have to consider the witness statement made by Merdan. And finally, the commander of the 3rd Corps implemented all possible missions in order to -- measures to engage in cooperation with all local authorities in order to solve the problem, such as, for example, the cooperation with the military police of the HVO as well as the civilian police. For example, they set up joint patrols, set up a joint commission, provided assistance within the framework of the work of that commission, and security measures were ensured by the battalion at the time of exchanges. The witness statement of Mr. Mujezinovic is quite valuable in this respect. The same goes for Merdan's witness statement, that of HF, as well as the press communique of the 3rd Corps dated the 15th of April. You should also refer to the conclusions approved by the War Presidency in Zenica dealing with the said situation. The effects are quite clear, Mr. President. There had been no advantage, no reason for the 3rd Corps to even envisage such an activity. What followed, Mr. President, was detrimental to the 3rd Corps, and it is for this reason that measures were undertaken in order to try and solve that situation as swiftly as possible. Why? Because as we have heard, one of the top priorities for General Hadzihasanovic was not to engage in any conflict with the HVO. It was a priority mission from his point of view. When the Prosecution says that those measures were aimed at obtaining more efficient control over the Mujahedin, well, we say the opposite. That is to say, that the evidence suggests that the Mujahedin on the territory of the 3rd Corps in 1993 were elements outside anyone's control, that they were loose cannons basically, and that the general was trying to find the best possible way to solve the problem under the prevailing circumstances at that particular moment in time. In order to just briefly refer to some of the measures implemented by General Hadzihasanovic, let me mention the security bodies of the 3rd Corps. They never stopped looking for information about these elements outside anyone's control and their activities in the course of the entire year, in the course of 1993. And the kidnapping of Totic triggered off a whole range of measures undertaken by the 3rd Corps in this respect. According to witnesses HF and HD, in spite of all their efforts in trying to gather as much as -- as much information as possible, everything they did was still insufficient. After the 15th of April, it was not possible for General Hadzihasanovic to solve this problem on his own considering the prevailing circumstances at the time. Witness Merdan, Witness ZB, Witness HD. On the 24th of April we had the events at Miletici. The problem of the Mujahedin was raised with the Supreme Command. Witness statement by Merdan. Measures were undertaken in order to obtain more information about those elements outside anyone's control. Witness statements by Sipic and Delalic, amongst others. In the month of May, the problem was once again raised with the Supreme Command in order to get some assistance. Witness ZB, Witness Merdan. The evidence suggests that the Mujahedin based at Poljanice were in touch with the Supreme Command with the aim of establishing a brigade which would be placed under the direct command of the Supreme Command. DH 278, DH 1007; Witness HF, Sipic and Delalic. The 8th of June, Maline. The security services implement other measures in order to obtain information in addition to all the measures what had already been implemented in order to determine who was responsible for the activities and crimes committed on that day. On the 13th of June, General Hadzihasanovic, since he was not happy with the lack of measures and lack of efficiency draws up a written report and asks for assistance in order to solve the problem of the Mujahedins. Witnesses Merdan, ZP; document DH 167.1 -- 165, sorry. Then the reflections of Colonel Stewart when reading this document. He was an experienced military man who had experience in Bosnia, who was quite marked by that, and he was familiar with the military terminology. When he looked at that report. He said this is an exoneration basically. He understood as a military man under how much stress General Hadzihasanovic had to work, what was the burden he was carrying on his shoulders, and he reacted by asking for measures to be implemented in order to do away with the problem of the Mujahedin. The question of the 3rd front is something that we'll come back to. The Mujahedin, on the other hand, and we know it on the basis of this evidence, refused to negotiate with the 3rd Corps. They refused to negotiate with General Hadzihasanovic. They wanted to deal with someone who was higher up. Who is higher up? We're not certain. Witness ZB, on the 25th of June -- on the 27th of June, said that the Mujahedin were not under effective control and the Presidency's dealing with the problem. As opposed to what I said yesterday with regard to the press talks and press encounter, it was not something which had been prepared beforehand. It happened by chance the witness was going through Zenica, and he thought he recognised the witness ZP. He wanted to ask him some questions and he got an answer immediately, on the spot. The authorisation from the Supreme Command issued to a person called Mahmuljin to try and get in touch with the Mujahedin and start negotiating with them. And then there was a proposal on the part of this Mahmuljin in order to set up the El Mujahid detachment and the order was issued by the Supreme Command in order for such a unit to be set up, and then there were certain difficulties in carrying out that order. All those events are described in great detail by witnesses Poparic, Merdan, ZP. And then we had resubordination of 336th Brigade which had not been carried out according to witnesses Merdan, Siljak, ZP, and HF. And so that concludes what we have to say on this issue. Mr. President, when I first made my opening statement, I did say that we are not denying that there were certain foreign elements present in Bosnia. You heard witnesses who saw them, but we also said that you would hear those witnesses tell you that those foreign elements were not under the actual and effective control of the 3rd Corps, that they were not a part of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina but that measures had been implemented in order to try and sort out this problem. We kept our word. The witnesses came along. The documents had been filed and the theory put forward by the Prosecution is -- by the Defence, sorry, is compatible with everything you have heard and everything you saw in those documents. There had never been any effective control over the Mujahedin. And the last witness statement, Cordy-Simpson, with regard to a question asked of him: "[In English] What do you expect a corps commander to do for crimes committed by people who are not your subordinates?" [Interpretation] And General Cordy-Simpson thought about his answer and said: "[In English] ... report the matter higher, that there is some force that is behaving outside his control in his area. He has no ability because he has no command function over someone who is not under his command. "It is a fundamental military principle and one that we, certainly where I have been, you have to establish exactly your command relationships with everyone in your area. And I don't want to confuse people, but there's a huge difference in being opcon," [Interpretation] which means operational control, "[In English] ... operational command, and for me it would be one of the first things that I would establish, whether forces in my area were opcom or not. "Now, that's easy because I come from an organisation that has brought up under Staff College trainings and all the rest of. It isn't quite so easy in the confused situation that we are talking about in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "I don't believe that if a force is operating which is not under your operational command there is much you can do when they get out of control." [Interpretation] In spite of this answer, Mr. President, which corresponds to Stewart's reaction and the report sent by General Hadzihasanovic to the Supreme Command, he sent this report. He asked for assistance. He asked for a reaction on the part of the Supreme Command. He asked his superiors to find a solution to the problem, what are your stances and opinion. All the measures were taken. Everyone was involved in the matter, and contrary to what the Prosecution claims, the purpose of all this work was to find a solution to the problem. The measures taken demonstrate the extent to which one attempted to solve a problem. To what extent one attempted to prevent these elements which were outside of control to have an adverse affect on the 3rd Corps and on the war. General Karavelic analysed the situation and reached the same conclusion. First, he said no, initially there is no problem. There is information. And then Totic appears. The matter became a little more serious. Perhaps that would affect the mission. And then we have the events in Miletici, and in that case it was something that had to be considered. The HVO was involved. The general had to react, and he explain the manner which the general reacted. Then we have the events in Maline, Guca Gora, and on each occasion, as the problem grows more serious, the measures taken by the 3rd Corps and the Supreme Command on all levels are more serious. They try to take more serious measures to deal with a problem that is increasingly unacceptable. The general, General Karavelic, said that he had reached an interesting conclusion. "[In English] The creation of this detachment," [Interpretation] he's referring to El Mujahid, "[In English] What other measures taken by the 3rd Corps appeared to have ended the perpetration of crimes by these foreigners. Without compromising the accomplishment of the mission the 3rd Corps, I am of the opinion that this is a striking example of very effective exercise of command at the strategic operative level." [Interpretation] What is a commander of an army corps demanded to do, especially when the corps does not even exist? He is asked to create the corps and to put in place a certain system, to have a deputy commander for security who will be involved in security matters, to have an assistant commander for operations who will be involved in operations. He is demanded to have assistant commander for logistics, to have an assistant commander for morale. He is demanded to have an assistant commander for legal affairs. He is demanded to create a legal department and establish permanent guidelines and instructions. He must sure there is an exchange of information within the 3rd Corps. He must ensure that subordinates are trained. The subordinate commanders must also be answerable to the corps commander. I can't think of the English term; I apologise. That is what a corps commander is requested to do. He must do all these things in order to accomplish his mission, when accomplishing his commission, and at the same time his legal obligations must be respected, and this is what General Hadzihasanovic did throughout 1993. And General Karavelic concluded by making a comparison with what he did in Sarajevo. He said that he went a little further. He took armed measures against a certain brigade, but he added: "[In English] While I was able to take measures regarding this brigade, it should be noted that it was officially in the composition of the 1st Corps," [Interpretation] an official brigade. "[In English] This happened on a very small area,"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: More information and my actions were approved by the Presidency of the republic and performed in cooperation with civilian authorities."
