[Interpretation] All of these elements were present in Sarajevo, and he went a little further when taking action when compared to the action taken by General Hadzihasanovic, but he also explained that in the territory of the 3rd Corps, given all the elements present and the context in which the 3rd Corps operated, he explained that such measures could not be envisaged, and this has been confirmed when one talks about plans for a month that are secret in order to face up to certain foreign elements. So this is the real situation. Mr. President, this is not just a theory. This is what took place in the field. This is what is supported by the evidence. There was no effective control. The notorious Mujahedin were not under the control of the 3rd Corps. And if a unit is not under the control of the 3rd Corps in order to try and respond to the arguments presented by the Prosecution or, rather, to contradict their arguments, if a crime is committed, it is the commander's responsibility to carry out an investigation. He carries out an investigation. He's satisfied that the individuals who committed the crime are not his subordinates. If this is done, then legally speaking that is the end of the matter. In terms of operational matters, he can go further, he can decide to go further, and he did go further. But as far as legal matters are concerned, that's the end of the affair unless the Chamber thinks that his decision was completely unreasonable. But if you have a look at the information that he had at that time, since he takes the reasonable decision that the crimes were not committed by his subordinates, well, as soon as this is done, then in legal terms that's the end of the matter. When we refer to the Mujahedin attacks -- well, on numerous occasions we have discussed the matter with witnesses. It was said that the Mujahedin had to be attacked. But if one needs to attack the Mujahedin, well, then, the conclusion to be drawn is that they're not under our control. If one believes that it's necessary to attack them, that means that they're not under his control. And the decision to attack them or not is not a legal decision, it is not a legal obligation. This is part of the operational mission, and this is why high-level commanders take decisions at a high level, decisions on whether having evaluated the situation one should conclude that's a third front, and I'm not capable of dealing with this. Is that a fabricated argument, or is this an argument that we can support by evidence? He has spoken to his superior and said, "It's my third front," and this is not an excuse invented by the Defence in the course of these proceedings. This is contained in the evidence, and it is supported by witness testimony. Thank you, Mr. President. I will now give the floor to my colleague who will deal with the charges in the indictment. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As we said yesterday, the Prosecution in this case has tried to take a narrow approach in relation to the entire case. My colleague has presented the Defence's opinion with regard to the duties of a commander and with regard to his responsibilities and the measures he has to take when crimes are committed in his territory. And this is not in dispute. It's accepted by the Defence in the territory of the 3rd Corps, and you have visited some of this territory. Crimes were committed. There were victims. We are aware of the fact today. In our trial brief, Mr. President, we provided a detailed analysis of all of the counts contained in the indictment, and we pointed out certain evidence that demonstrates that with regard to the charges in the indictment, the Prosecution has not provided sufficient evidence that would show that Commander Hadzihasanovic failed to carry out his obligations as a commander, the obligations he should have carried out since he was legally bound to do so in terms of local and international law. When presenting the facts today, I intend to focus only on some issues raised by the Prosecution in its brief or in its oral submissions. I'll start with Dusina. Your Honours, many witnesses have testified about Dusina, and the Defence and the Prosecution have presented a lot of written evidence to you with regard to Dusina. You know about the context in which the events in Dusina took place. You have before you evidence about the situation that Commander Hadzihasanovic found himself in as soon as he arrive in the area. He came from Sarajevo and believed that he would be an integral part of the armed forces of the Bosnia and Herzegovina together with the HVO. He was aware of the fact that given that the army had not been established and was scattered around the territory that he had arrived in. I will remind you of the fact that the witness Ibrakovic said in Zenica alone there were 134 armed groups, and he was aware of the fact that as a professional soldier he should suggest to his colleague Colonel Blaskic that they should create a professional force in order to discipline the troops. He immediately had a problem. His request was rejected. That is in the evidence. And the entire state of Bosnia and Herzegovina wanted to lift the blockade of Sarajevo. His request to the commander of the operative zone was rejected, so the reaction was identical to the reaction of the HVO. He could have been very disappointed. The commander could have been very disappointed, but the commander was subjected to fierce attacks from the territory of Gornji Vakuf, from the territory of Prozor, and from the Zenica area. Many witnesses have testified about the context, but I will mention Edin Husic, who was the deputy commander for intelligence, the assistant commander for intelligence, and he spoke about large forces coming from Western Herzegovina to the Lasva Valley territory. He then mentioned the attack on Busovaca, and he mention add new wave of refugees moving in the direction of Zenica. Commander Hadzihasanovic's priority task was to protect the Lasva junction at that point in time. That was the only route that could be used to establish communication with the other free territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, the HVO had already blocked the main road, thinking Zenica to Travnik in the Lasva Valley not far from the Lasva junction, they had attacked Busovaca. They started expelling the population from those areas. And on the 25th of January, Merdani was also attacked, which was located only a few kilometres from Lasva. Given such a situation, we agree with the Prosecution's position. Commander Hadzihasanovic, although had not it not been for the Lasva junction then the battle might not be a battle that would require the engagement of Commander Hadzihasanovic, but Commander Hadzihasanovic did all he could to ensure that the junction was protected. I won't mention evidence that has been shown to witnesses on numerous occasions, but he issued orders in order to secure the only small route that we have used in order to make it possible for troops and people to move around freely. But the lines that had not been taken by the enemy, elevation 852 and the Dusina-Sudine route, should be secured without engaging in combat. We have heard the witness Barucija, the witness Begic who took those forces through a route that didn't pass through five checkpoints established by the HVO from the railway station in Vlasenica towards the village of Dusina. This was done in order to avoid any clashes, so as not to provoke any clashes. So General Hadzihasanovic performed his duties, tried to accomplish his mission, and he did everything he could do to avoid provoking a conflict with the HVO. Unfortunately, a conflict did break out after one of the commanders of the 7th Muslim Brigade, Camdzic, was killed. And I won't say anything else about this matter. I will now go back to what the Prosecutor said in his closing argument. The Prosecutor said that Commander Hadzihasanovic immediately found out about the murders and didn't take the necessary measures although he had all the resources that he required to do so. Firstly, he referred to Exhibit P135, public announcement, and he said that he saw that Zvonko Rajic, the commander of the Lasva HVO, had been killed. He had such information. Mr. President, we have already had translation problems. In our language there is a quite clear distinction between the word "kill" and die a violent death. Someone can be killed with a certain intention or accidentally. To die a violent death is something that can happen in a traffic accident or in the course of combat. So this public announcement only stated that Zvonko Rajic died a violent death in the course of combat on that day in Lasva. The Prosecution -- the Prosecution arguments with regard to this document are not founded. However, nothing says that Commander Hadzihasanovic was not aware of the event. His deputy, General Merdan who attended the meeting together with the HVO that evening, a meeting at which Commander Blaskic expressed suspicion that the delegation had been killed, and he said that village with Croatian population had been torched, the population had been expelled, et cetera, and he did not want to sign a cease-fire agreement, an agreement on a cease-fire in Busovaca. His deputy informed him of the fact, and this can be seen from the information that he also provided to the Supreme Command Staff. The information was quite identical. The commander found out about the allegations made by the enemy. And as a reasonable commander, he gathered all information from his units that participated in that combat, and all the information that we have in evidence shows that combat broke out, this had not been planned or ordered. In the course of that combat, a number of individuals died a violent death in -- on both sides. There are certain contradictions contained in those reports, but since the corps was only just being established, only had a month had passed since he assumed his duties, well, if we take into consideration the difficulty of providing the information, and if we take in consideration the difficulties of the work of the operations centre and the difficulty of communications, witnesses have testified about this, if we take all this into consideration, then if there are certain things that don't tally in the reports, this is not surprising. Reports from his own units that should be trusted by a commander, but a commander should also check such reports, well, General Merdan provided such reports on the following day at the meeting, and there were no issues raised by the HVO with regard to that event. What measures did the commander take? Not because he didn't have information according to which the suspicions of the enemy were not correct, it's not as if he thought he could stop -- well, the witnesses before this court have explained what kind of information he had. The witness General Merdan said that we took this seriously into consideration because this was the first time that there was -- that the members of the ABiH were suspected of having committed a crime, and as a result we paid particular attention to this problem. And General Merdan, together with the HVO members and members of the internationality community, went into the field. From the witness Barucija, who has testified here, and from other soldiers in that area, he heard the same story that had been conveyed to him in reports from subordinate units. They saw people there, Bosniaks and Croats, people who were afraid as recorded in an HVO report which stated at that Mr. Fleming said that it seemed that something had happened. General Merdan said, yes, it was quite certain that they were afraid. That was the first time that the war actually entered their houses and there were victims. But no one said that any sort of crime had been committed. The next step taken -- Dusina and Merdan continued to be shelled from HVO positions on the next day, but the next step taken was the sanitation of the area, and as one of the witness's has testified, bodies were taken to the Zenica morgue. The investigative judge was informed. He immediately went to the site, and according to the evidence two judges went there, Mirsad Strika and Vlado Adamovic, investigative judges. Given the fact that a military police battalion was only formed in mid-January 1993, although there is a decision that was taken in December, so to take -- to carry out investigations, on-site investigations, to carry out investigations in Zenica, which is not the actual site, well, with regard to these investigations the judge did everything he could. An external examination of the bodies was performed. The paraffin glove test was carried out. The bodies were identified. An order was issued to military police members according to which they should take interviews from individuals, interrogate individuals who had been brought in. The witness Saric has testified here and said that he personally interrogated Zvonko Rajic's brother. None of this evidence with regard to how the people died a violent death, with regard to the wounds, with regard to the paraffin glove test, et cetera. None of the evidence obtained when the legal procedure was followed, the legal procedure of which the judge was in charge and not someone from the ABiH or Commander Hadzihasanovic. None of the evidence showed that the previous reports from the units of the ABiH were not correct. All the material was provided to the prosecutor, and it was then for the prosecutor to act. It was for the prosecutor to decide whether there were any other elements that had to be checked. It's quite obvious that at the time the prosecutor did not believe that anything else should be checked. When there were any doubts, he shelved that. So everything that is provided for by a legal system, by the criminal procedure, all the roles that had to be played by the various bodies at that point of time were played. Everything was checked. All the doubts that the enemy had were checked. Nothing was found that would contradict what people in the field said. Nothing contradicted the statements, the written statements made by the units that participated in the combat. So today in 2005, not in 1995 but today in 2005, if the same bodies were involved in such an affair and obtained the same information, a prosecutor in any country would probably act in a similar way. Why were eye-witnesses not interrogated? It's difficult to say who the eye-witnesses were. The people who were frightened had already left and went to Zenica. A few days later they went to a territory under the control of the HVO, and there was not a single ABiH organ or a single civilian body or body of power that took charge of the matter. Not a single such body had access to that territory. So these people could only be interrogated by the competent state organ of the HVO. The Prosecutor presented evidence according to which the HVO and its security services only one year later filed a criminal report against a certain number of individuals, although they had access to all those who could have provided other information that couldn't be obtained by the official authorities in Zenica, couldn't be obtained by the police or by the judicial bodies. The Prosecutor goes on to say that the information that was taken from prisoners or detainees was just the usual information that you take from any detainee. We don't know on the basis of what facts regarding this case the Prosecution managed to draw this conclusion. We heard two witnesses here, Witness Izet Mahir who was ferrying the detainees from Lasva to KP Dom, and he took an interest in their condition, but he never heard from anyone that they were mistreated or anything about what had happened. And as to the question: Is it normal that somebody who is detained is afraid of those who detain him and don't want to say anything, he answered that question in an affirmative. He said that it was normal. So it is indeed normal that those people, even if they had the knowledge of certain facts, would not tell the police officers interrogating them of those facts. But you can't blame the police officers for that. You also know that one of the witnesses said that at the school he met with his wife and that he whispered to her and told her about this event and asked her not to tell anyone, and he just said this to her in order to be informed in case anything happened to him. So under realistic conditions, the investigation had been carried out in line with the legal provisions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. No body, either the accords or the prosecutors or anyone else could have reached that conclusion. And Commander Hadzihasanovic who was the one who actually initiated all this flurry of activity had no further competence to start interfering with the proceedings of the judiciary without an express request on the part of the judiciary for the armed forces to start implementing any new additional measures. Because of the fact that you do have information about the criminal code of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the law on the judiciary and you are familiar with all that, it is simply unbelievable that the Prosecution still sticks to its original position according to which nothing whatsoever had been done. And this is not all. They go back to an image of the legal system which has been turned upside down. For example, they keep telling us about this famous cow, somebody coming from Switzerland, they would have nothing against it. I mean, they're asking why no investigation had been carried out here and that the investigation had been carried out. And we heard from the witness Veseljak. And what he was trying to say was that the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the 3rd Corps were ready and willing, and this happened even after the disarming of 306th Brigade. They were willing to undertake any measures against their soldiers in case they were found to be putting the lives of Croat population in jeopardy or endangering their property. They set up checkpoints. They brought in reinforcements. And even if we look at something which is from our point of view perhaps a minor affair, but for any farmer a cow is not a minor affair. So it doesn't really matter what they did. But what does matter was that they were willing to impose force. They were willing to even shoot their own soldiers because they put the lives of their fellow citizens into jeopardy because they were fighting for a multi-ethnic state of Bosnia, and this fight was incorporated in every single policy of the 3rd Corps, that everything had to be done in order to make sure that their soldiers in no way could endanger civilians. Religious leaders, religious facilities, in case they were found to be doing so, strict measures had to be imposed. And it is for this reason that with regard to the case of Dusina, the case that we referred to earlier on, let me just reiterate the position that in this case, following the information that perhaps a crime might have been committed by members of the armed forces, the commander of the 3rd Corps in line with the legal provisions of Bosnia and Herzegovina undertook all the necessary and indispensable measures and even more than that, and that at the time he did not obtain any information indicating that there was reasonable suspicion that such a crime had been perpetrated. We are simply reiterating what we already put to you in writing. The Prosecution did not even manage to prove that Serif Patkovic did indeed kill Zvonko Rajic. The witnesses who spoke about that did not know Serif Patkovic, Zeljko Cvijanovic. Cvijanovic is a person you cannot trust, quite apart from the fact that he is a suspect for having killed another person and having thus provoked the conflict in Dusina. And he contradicted himself on a number of occasions, so you can tell immediately that it's not a credible witness. So nobody who was an eye-witness recognised Patkovic. In the Blaskic case, Rajic's wife claimed that she saw Patkovic. Patkovic testified before the same Trial Chamber, and he said that he wasn't there and that he did not commit that murder. And there is a case at Zenica, and Judge Adamovic is in charge of that case, and he came and testified here. And the wife of Zvonko Rajic did testify before that judge. And Kozaric mentioned this, and that's why I'm mentioning this, not because I've heard it from any other source. And she said that the wife of Zvonko Rajic before the court of Zenica said clearly that her husband had not been killed by Serif Patkovic. So as to the first count of the indictment, the Defence, with all due respect, states that there is not a single piece of evidence pointing to any responsibility that should be borne by the commander of the 3rd Corps. The situation is fairly similar when it comes to Miletici. In relation to Miletici, all I'm going to say is the following: All evidence that we have seen here does not provide us with an even -- with even a shred of suspicion that the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina might have participated in this. The evidence provided for in -- from international staff and a part of that evidence was provided by the HVO, and especially the evidence that the Defence presented here through witnesses, indicates that everything was done in order to save the lives of the Croat population and all evidence indicates that that crime was perpetrated by the Mujahedin. As my learned colleague has said, at that moment the legal obligation when it came to any military commander starting from Zukanovic at Mehurici all the way to Commander Hadzihasanovic actually ceased. He was accountable for the deeds of those subordinated to him over whom he had an effective command and control. However, as in no other case, here too we can say that Commander Hadzihasanovic and the subordinated units were not satisfied with the situation because it tarnished the image of the armed forces, and it had a negative effect on the morale of their soldiers, and it was for this reason that he undertook other measures and actions, not because he had a legal obligation to do so or because he had failed to do anything he was supposed to do, because there is no failure to act on his part. So he informed his superiors of that event. He asked for authorisation to gather information about those groups who were creating problems for him in that area. He employed special security officers who were entrusted with the fact of dealing with African elements only. And also his chief of security in the 306th Brigade was instructed to start gathering information on those individuals and to keep him posted at all times. According to what Dedo Suljic said in his statement of 92 bis, some individuals came along and asked him for information as to what had happened, and he told him everything he told us in 92 bis. Commander Sipic, together with his chief of security, attempted to enter the camp at Poljanice and to find out who those people were and what they were up to in an area inhabited by his people but he never managed to do so. So with regard to this event, too, even though after the indisputable fact confirming that this crime was perpetrated by the Mujahedin, a number of other measures had been undertaken, had been implemented, in order to prevent them from acting in the same way again. The fact is that they were not end an effective command of control as proven by witnesses Siljak and Sulejman who mentioned the fact that had they been within the framework of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina we wouldn't have had to negotiate with them. We would have been able to issue orders to them. As to the events at Maline, I would also like to draw Your Honours' attention to everything you have heard from the witnesses and to the exhibits which had been filed, the evidence that has been accepted by you, in fact. A man came here who had been faced with the perpetrators of that crime. He was actually not an eye-witness to the crime itself, but he was the person who had been in a situation whereby a number of people who he had been taking from Maline to Mehurici had been taken away by force and kidnapped. Now, the question arises as to whether he was acting with a lack of caution by taking 200 people near Poljanice. When we visited the area, we did see that any shortcut to Mehurici went passed Poljanice. The only other way was through Han Bila about ten kilometres further through an area where there was fighting going on. And anyone in their right mind would have taken those people by the shortest possible route to a safe place. And as the witness replied in answer to your question, "I don't know even today whether I made the right decision, but I couldn't even imagine, couldn't even dream of those Mujahedin attacking us." So he was of the view that the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina were guaranteeing the safety of that Croat population, and that's why they were taking them there. Had they left them in the village, they might have been in danger. That was his assessment of the situation. As to what criterion, what conditions reigned is indicated in the evidence and in our written brief. And the situation is identical here. It is quite clear, Your Honours, on the basis all evidence that the Mujahedin and those who joined them, those locals who joined them, who were in disguise basically and who were not under the control of Bosnia-Herzegovina perpetrated that crime. So legally speaking, once again, at that particular point in time any obligation for any further investigation would have ceased. However, we do have evidence to indicate that Commander Hadzihasanovic and those subordinated to him went even beyond the call of duty. We have heard what the commander -- the police commander Zukanovic had to say. Throughout the following fortnight they were setting traps, so to say, and they were taken written statements from people who had been leading that group of people that had been taken by force, and they were looking for any other information in order to find out what had happened, where it had happened, and how it had happened in order to be able to make a suggestion to the competent authorities as to what measures should be implemented and in what way. But they also had a clear attitude from the corps commander, and General Cuskic testified about that here. He actually asked for that problem to be solved and to establish whether anyone who was a member of the armed forces had any part in it and, if so, for that person to be severely punished. So all efforts were made by the battalion. And if we think of the events at Guca Gora, further measures were implemented in the direction of the Supreme Command Staff in order for this problem to be solved as soon as possible, because it was beginning to have serious consequences to the detriment of the mission of Commander Hadzihasanovic. In relation to this event and other latter events, the Prosecutor established an assumption of a possible cover-up, because later on in the month of October when Mr. Mazowiecki asked the president of the Presidency and he in his turn asked through the Supreme Command Staff to investigate the situation at Maline, and the answer given was not quite in line with the facts established previously. General Merdan, who testified before this Trial Chamber and who sent the answer on behalf of the 3rd Corps to the Supreme Command Staff, was unable to tell us exactly for what reason he did that. Was it because Commander Hadzihasanovic was absent or away or otherwise engaged? But we do know that it was General Merdan who supplied the answer. General Merdan encountered this problem of the deaths at Maline on the 3rd of August for the first time, according to his testimony. It was on that occasion that some people in the area, and he was accompanied by the representatives of the European Community, and some people showed them the burial sites, the graves where these people were buried, and they said that they lost their lives in combat. And when he got the report from the brigade repeating the statement that he heard on the spot, he therefore had no doubt as to the truthfulness of that statement, and he felt no need to check it out any further. As to whether he should have been in touch with his security officers or not, but he received two identical pieces of information, and that's what was the basis for his answer. You can't qualify it as a cover-up. And as to whether the 306th Brigade was trying to cover it up in the period between the 8th of June, that is say, the time when the event happened, well, there had been quite a few organisational and other changes in the meantime in the area of responsibility of the 306th Brigade. On the basis of the war diaries you will see on the 19th of August there was a new commander who was replaced, and instead of Commander Sipic who was familiar with the facts a new commander came along who had no knowledge of the event. He asked for information from the security services, and as testified by witness Delalic here, he did not give that information in person, and he could not recognise the person who was briefing the then new commander Jusufspahic about the facts, and that was the information that was relayed to the 3rd Corps. The commander of the 306th Brigade was unable to check himself the events at Mehurici because the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade, which at the time of events was at Mehurici was no longer within the framework of the 306th Brigade. It was an integral part of the 27th Brigade which was set up in the middle of August. Unfortunately, considering the circumstances, this was the reason basically for the difference between the information in June and the information obtained later on. And General Merdan testified to the fact that he had never seen the letter that was addressed to the Supreme Command Staff, but he did know that there was a letter from them to the 3rd Corps and he tried to give an answer to the best of his ability and to the best of his knowledge, and he tried to give such an answer to every question asked by the Supreme Command Staff. This state of affairs which follows from the evidence in this case tell us once again that the Prosecution, in relation to this event in much the same way as in relation to the events taking place -- that took place at Miletici, did not manage to prove beyond reasonable doubt that those crimes were perpetrated by the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina or individuals who were under effective control and command of General Hadzihasanovic. All the measures that we have described earlier indicate that the commander and his officers and his services did even much more than was their legal obligation either according to the domestic or the international law. Your Honours, in relation to events which also have to do with Mehurici, I would just like to note for the sake of the transcript that even though in the written briefs the Prosecution referred to that as well as the prison at the JNA barracks in Travnik in the course of their oral presentation, they made no reference to those events. As to what the reasons are, they probably know best. And I would just like to refer to two crimes perpetrated by the Mujahedin, that is to say, the Guca Gora incident and the Travnik incident which took place at the Sveti Ilija church. The Prosecution also has certain claims about measures not taken here, and the commander is aware of what happened. If we listen to the witnesses Cusic and Mesanovic, we could see that not only at the time of the events but even prior to the events and in accordance with the general policies according to which religious buildings and members of the clergy should be protected, the municipal defence staff in Travnik ensured that the Catholic church was permanently protected as well as the house in which the priests lived, and they in fact showed that the attack on the church and their entry into the house and the attack on the soldiers guarding the priests was carried out by the Mujahedin. That is not in dispute. The civilian police also went to the site of the crime and filed a criminal report against unidentified perpetrators. So you can quite clearly see that it was for the civilian police to act at that point in time. However, the military organs also went to the site and provided assistance, and everything they did, they subsequently repaired the church, provided assistance, everything they did quite clearly shows that although this did not fall within their competence the army did more than was possible. As far as Guca Gora is concerned -- as far as Guca Gora is concerned, the evidence is also quite clear as well as the measures taken by the 3rd Corps. Although they were no longer legally obliged to take such measures, witnesses quite clearly stated that such measures were taken. But I would just like to comment on the Prosecution's position with regard to the army taking measures when religious buildings and cultural buildings belonging to the Croatian people are concerned. With regard to Guca Gora, they say that no measures were taken. Well, we didn't take measures. We didn't even photograph it. We first wanted to clean it up, but--

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now resume. It's five past 1.00. According to my calculations, the Defence has another one hour so please use your time as you see fit, but I should point out that we have to adjourn at quarter to because another trial is scheduled for 2.15. You have another hour available and you may use it as you see fit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there was something that I wanted to say before the break about the evidence with regard to item 7, the destruction or damage of buildings dedicated to religion. With regard to the other counts -- as in the case of the other counts in the indictment, I won't be analysing the evidence here. What is concerned is the monastery in Guca Gora and the church in Travnik. I have already addressed these matters to certain extent. As far as Guca Gora is concerned, Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to what our expert in history has said and the expert in constitutional matters has said. This had to do with a certain tradition in Bosnia-Herzegovina that was such that the inhabitants of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Bosniaks had a particular relationship when it came to protecting the buildings of other ethnic groups, that they would treat them as if they belonged to their own culture. A draft -- a report has been drafted about this by a representative of the United Nations, by Mr. Kaiser. As far as this relationship of the ABiH towards the religious buildings of other ethnic buildings are concerned, his statements were the same. You also have evidence according to which the commander issued special orders in which he attempted to protect the cultural and religious buildings of his co-inhabitants in order to accomplish the mission that he was assigned with in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in order to protect the multi-ethnic character of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As far as the monastery in Guca Gora is concerned, we dispose of facts according to which the items of value in the monastery were moved to Croatia in December 1992. It's also not in dispute that the Mujahedin entered the building. At one point in time they destroyed certain things in the monastery: The frescos, the organ and the statue in front of the monastery. The books were scattered around -- the remaining books from the library that hadn't been taken to the Republic of Croatia were scattered around. And you have heard witnesses who put all those books in order when the army entered the monastery. Library in order was also found by the delegation that Stjepan Radic was a member of on the 3rd of August. And the witness Franjo Krizanovic said that when in spring 1994 he took charge of the monastery and took over from General Alagic, he said that at that time the library was still in place. All of our inhabitants and citizens and especially the commander regret the fact that certain damage was inflicted on the church in Travnik and on the monastery in Guca Gora. And as a result of that damage, the religious and national sentiments of our co-inhabitants were offended, but what we heard from witnesses and what we saw at the site in legal terms does not amount to the destruction or wilful damage inflicted on religious buildings as provided for by international law. On the contrary. All the evidence points to the fact that the utmost measures were taken. A special military police battalion was engaged and a police force from that area was engaged to prevent other damage from being inflicted. And as the witness Karic has stated, when the roof was damaged from HVO positions, the ABiH carried out the necessary repairs. All of these efforts made, and this is part of our culture, and all of the obligations and duties of the commander. All of these efforts, all of the obligations and duties of the commander were misrepresented in the Prosecution's closing argument when they addressed the protection of religious buildings in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The question was put, "You didn't photograph the monastery? You could have done so." But, Your Honours, in order to distinguish those who committed crimes, the commander issued an order according to which everyone had to have identity cards. The witnesses then said that they were confronted with a problem because there was no film, there was no paper in order to make such identity cards. So in certain conditions when a religious building belonging to the Croats was under threat, the army did everything to prevent it from being destroyed and it wasn't destroyed. It's just that a threat was posed to this building. And this was done when, during the very same period, not far from that building, Muslim religious buildings were completely destroyed. You will remember the testimony of witness Kent-Payne who said that he went to Bandol and there was no indication on the map of the location of the mosque. He found a pile of rubble there. It was not far from Velika Bukovica. And one month earlier on the village of Ahmici had been completely destroyed, together with the mosque. It's not only that no revenge was taken, but additional efforts were made to ensure that not a single individual, not a single member of the ABiH should feel the desire to treat Croatian religious and cultural buildings in a similar way. In their address the Prosecution said -- in its opening statement the Prosecution said the commander can do everything. He can ask why one and a half litres of petrol was stolen or -- and a car in Kraljeva Sutjeska. But naturally we always have to go back to the concrete conditions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Kraljeva Sutjeska is the best-known monument of the Croatian culture and religion in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We have in evidence information, according to which when conflict broke out in Kakanj, General Hadzihasanovic issued a special order according to which if combat continued in the direction of Kraljeva Sutjeska, everything should be done to protect to the monastery. When he heard after the combat that not a litre and a half was stolen but one and a half tonnes of oil was stolen, he asked for a commission to be formed, for measures to be taken, and the commander of the 3rd Muslim Brigade provided information and said that all the measures had been taken and the commander who was engaged in combat in the area had been replaced and all the resources had been returned to the monastery. We don't know what the theory of the Prosecution is. Is it good if we take all measures both before and after, or is it good when we do not immediately manage to prevent partial damage from being inflicted? We are not sure when a commander has complied with all his duties and when he hasn't. So as far as item 7 is concerned, count 7 is concerned, although I regret the fact that the national and religious feelings of our co-inhabitants have been offended, that the damage inflicted on these buildings do not satisfy the criteria that would enable one to say that a crime was committed. On the other hand, both crimes were committed by the Mujahedin, and the 3rd Corps commander had no authority over them and they were not his subordinate men and he did not have effective control over them. In addition, he took all the necessary measures in order to protect those buildings. And for these reasons and with regard to this count in the indictment, it is our belief that the Prosecution has failed to prove that this act was actually committed. I will now go back to counts 5 and 6, wanton destruction of towns, villages, and that is not justified by necessity. Our legal position is one that we have mentioned in our previous briefs, in our previous submissions. But with regard to this count I would like to say the following: In the course of proceedings and in the course of their opening statement, the Prosecution has tried to provide the Chamber with facts that are correct and that are not in dispute. The Prosecution has presented us with a picture of the situation in the year 2000. We don't know who made the situation such, but the Defence has brought individuals before this Tribunal from the civilian protection in Travnik and in Zenica whose responsibility it was to protect buildings in territory after combat. And we have also provided documents from that time drafted on the 23rd of July, 1993. And on the basis of the information available at the time there was a description for each village of the buildings that were damaged and of the nature of the damage. And, Your Honours, in all of the evidence that you have before you, the damage does not reach the level -- a level that could be described as wanton destruction in accordance with international criteria. If his subordinates had committed such acts, a commander would be held responsible for them. On the other hand, given the way in which torching was carried out, destruction was inflicted on property and property was stolen, well, nothing has been proven by the Prosecution in this respect. In that very vast area that you have seen which is not very accessible, we don't know where all the refugees went. We don't know the routes that they used. We don't know where the troops went during the day and at night. We don't know where the buildings were located or where the civilian and military police tried to protect the area. We don't know who acted and how they acted. We don't know why this destruction was inflicted, what the destruction was a result was, whether it was a result of the combat that was ongoing throughout the summer or whether it was the result of certain individuals who were not unidentified acting on their own. But you have heard from witnesses that efforts were made to shed light on all of this, and the witness Saric has testified about this. We showed him examples of two cases of houses being torched and army members were held to account for these acts. But they were held responsible for posing a general danger to individuals and property. This concerned torching the property of Croatian inhabitants. So when the member of the army was identified, he was prosecuted. In the Strugar case, the Trial Chamber concluded that it was only if destruction had been proved beyond a reasonable doubt that such destruction is something that the commander could then be charged with. The Prosecution hasn't provided us with any evidence that would prove beyond any doubt that a member of the army set fire to a certain building. So since the Prosecution has not provided such evidence, and since there are a lot of doubts as to the identity of the individuals involved in torching certain buildings, we believe that General Hadzihasanovic should be acquitted on this count in the indictment. And why what was detected wasn't qualified as a war crime is something that we have spoken about on a number of occasions to our colleagues who have appeared before this Tribunal, who said that you are prosecuted on the basis of an event and the event concerned is something that is described or legally qualified by a court. In response to a question put to the judge, Veseljak, when he was asked why such-and-such an act was described as a case of theft and not of war crime pursuant to Article 142, he said that if someone's house was set on fire he would use the house -- the roof or the window of another house that had been abandoned. So from his point of view, he didn't understand why we asked him why he wanted to take the roof from an abandoned house to use for his own house. We know that some people misappropriated property when this was essential, but we prosecuted them in spite of the fact. And many of the criminal reports that we have shown you relate to such events and such individuals. This was a matter of necessity for them at the time. It was necessary to investigate such crimes and to punish the perpetrators, and this is the least that the 3rd Corps could do, and Commander Hadzihasanovic. So, Your Honours, you have all the information regarding these counts before you, and the Defence believes that the Prosecution has failed to prove that General Hadzihasanovic is guilty on this count and he should be acquitted on this count. I'm still left with a couple of things I have to say about prisons. First of all, Mr. President, in the course of our expert witness testimony on military matters and in his report it was explained in great detail what the responsibilities of a commander are with regard to any detention facilities. He indicated the difference between the responsibilities of the corps commander and commanders at different -- at other, different levels of command. Similar questions were put to General Merdan, and in an almost identical way General Merdan replied to those questions. For these reasons -- I'm not going to go into all the various legal duties and obligations for a corps commander, because the Defence fully agrees with the reasons indicated in the expert witness report and also indicated in his testimony before this Trial Chamber. As to the music school, which is situated in the centre of the city of Zenica not far from the civilian police station, the municipal and higher civilian courts in the vicinity of the municipal offices and a little bit further away from the 3rd Corps command, about two kilometres away, it seems to follow from the evidence that some persons had been detained and mistreated there. The Prosecution seems to indicate that it happened before the eyes of the 3rd Corps commander and that it was a widely known fact. Such a position is based on the account of one witness, the judge Vlado Adamovic, who supposedly was able to see all that from his windows, and we see when we visited the location that it was in fact impossible for him to see any such thing. And apparently it was also mentioned by family members of those people who had been detained at the music school. The Defence does not argue against the fact that some people were indeed detained at the music school, and it is not really relevant that Judge Vlado Adamovic knew about that, but as opposed to his testimony we also have the testimony from witness Kulovic, from witness Jasarevic, from witness Mirsad Mesic who told this Court that it wasn't a widely known fact. Witness Kulovic was a personal friend of Stipan Radic, and the same applies to witness Mirsad Mesic, and they testified to the fact that Stipan Radic never mentioned this problem to them. Who would a member of the clergy confide in and ask for assistance from if not from his friends who were extremely influential in Zenica in spite of the fact that the Prosecution says that it would be inappropriate for us to say that Judge Adamovic should have reported information that he heard from people who complained to him. We continue to stick to the position that we have explained before. Had the situation been as drastic as Judge Vlado Adamovic says they had been, it would have been normal for a judge not to discuss this over coffee with his colleague, the district military prosecutor, but he would have to officially accept a criminal report from the person who had informed him of the facts and follow this route. In defence of the judge, Vlado Adamovic, even though we think it would have been normal for him to start proceedings in this way, the Prosecution actually is saying that not just him but anybody else, all the other citizens and the commander would have been obliged to report a crime had they known about it. Of course I do know that this is a widely existing obligation for any citizen, but it is not just for the commander to do. Just as according to the Prosecution the commander would have been called upon to do that, it would have applied to the chief of police as well and especially a judge. The fact that they did not proceed to do that is the best possible piece of evidence we can get to indicate that the problem was not so severe in Zenica as the Prosecution seems to claim, together with Judge Adamovic and some other witnesses. However, no matter what the scope of the problem, the Defence is well aware of the fact that the witnesses did refer to the fact that they had been detained there and mistreated there. Such information did in fact reach the commander, and he implemented necessary and reasonable measures. But those were rumours, not reports or complaints from any actual person who had been detained and mistreated. Well, in that case he would have checked the information. But as testified to by members of the military police battalion and the military security services, the information was sought and requested from the police whose offices were in the vicinity. What they received by way of an answer was that some people were indeed taken in in line with legal provisions, if they were suspected of some infringement or crime, but that those people were not mistreated. In the same way, measures were undertaken, the deputy commander, the security chief of their own accord and together with the representatives of the international community visited the music school on a number of occasions, and they found no evidence of any mistreatment having taken place there. The international witness Baggesen testified to the fact that he himself visited the entire premises of the school and that he found no trace whatsoever of any such thing, and he did not actually see any prisoners either, and especially no trace of any torture having taken place there. As to whether it might have been done in a -- some kind of illegal and underhand way, I'm not going to speculate on that, but the commander did undertake measures. And the representatives of the international community did have access, and such checks as carried out by the international community members did not point to the fact that any further criminal proceedings had to be instituted against any of the people in charge of the facility. And as was testified here, apart from witness Baggesen, we've also got the accepted facts claimed by Witness HI who in a way similar to that adopted by Mr. Baggesen referred to his own visit to the music school. And as we heard from the witness, since the policy of the 3rd Corps was to institute criminal proceedings against anyone guilty of crime, had there been any conditions justifying that, that is to say, if in 1993 the commander and his staff had received information that anyone at all was actually guilty of mistreatment and abused the prisoners at the music school, criminal proceedings would have been instituted against any such person. As to the Mehurici school, even though as I've said before the Prosecution has not referred to that in the course of their presentation, we are of the view that the civilians were taken there for their own safety and that the military was not in charge of them but the military was doing all they possibly could in order to assist the civilian authorities in providing housing and accommodation and anything else, and they enabled the Red Cross staff to come and see them immediately. And as we heard from witness Ivic, it would have been a shame to say that those people were not given fair treatment. As to Kovanica, the Prosecution did not offer a shred of evidence to indicate that -- that General Hadzihasanovic had any knowledge of such a place, that is to say, the blacksmith's shop even existing. It is quite obvious that many bad things happened there. Bugojno is the place which is geographically the farthest away from the 3rd Corps, and it was really almost inaccessible. And in 1993 it was a part of the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps that could only be reached by winding mountain path that we could only glimpse somewhere far away in the mountains. And there was an operational group there of the brigade of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As in all other cases, it is clear here, too, that combat activity did not take place in the way as the Prosecution is claiming, that is to say, that the armed forces launched an all-out attack on Croat towns and villages, but things happened in the way in which you were told about by witnesses. More specifically, at Bugojno, in spite of all efforts to avoid conflict after the events at Vrbanja, the conflict spread to the entire city. Since the conflict was taking place in a town where there was no prison or detention facility and large sections of the HVO had been disarmed, considering all that, there was a need for some kind of a facility where these people could be placed until they could be transferred to the KP Dom at Zenica in line with the policies of the 3rd Corps. However, this did not happen on the basis of the documentary evidence that we've got, and that's for two reasons, one reason being one of the protected witnesses who testified to that, who is an intellectual from Bugojno, and he said that they wrote special letters to the fact that they did not want people from Bugojno to be transferred to Zenica. If they had to be tried, they had to be tried at Bugojno because they were afraid that when travelling to Zenica they could come to grief. On the other hand, there are objective reasons indicated in the report, that is to say, that there were not sufficient means of transport in order to transfer all those people. And thirdly, when travelling to Zenica, they would have had to go through areas where there was combat activity going on all the time. And in line with the Geneva Convention about the protection of war prisoners, the transfer of war prisoners can own be carried out if there is full safety and security for that transport. All of those were probably the reasons why in addition to the reason at that particular time there was an agreement reached between the three warring parties and that there would be a full-scale exchange programme, and so the detained Croat members were therefore kept at Bugojno. In relation to the evidence in our possession, we can claim with a great deal of certainty that the grammar school facility which at a later date was returned to the civilian authorities for their own use was at no time under the control of the members of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As to the conditions in those facilities, we have two types of information there. One type of information was provided by the former detainees, and the other type was found in the reports drawn up by the European Monitors, and they carried out assessments of the situation in Bugojno on a regular basis. And we also have a report from Rudy Gerritsen to which I would like to draw your attention to in particular, and he does refer to satisfactory conditions, the fact that those people appeared to be well. And where the situation was most dire at the furniture warehouse, he did say that there was a couple of puddles of water on -- on the -- on the floor of that furniture salon. And then there were two cases of death. In relation to Mario Zrno, we have proof that indicated clearly that he was carrying out permissible and permitted duties for a prisoner at the cemetery at Zenica, and the evidence indicates that the civilians had mistreated him quite badly, civilians who were there to bury their relatives. And one of the Prosecution witnesses testified to the fact that there were two military police officers guarding him and that they were unable to -- to protect the prisoners from those civilians. Mario Zrno died of his injuries, but let me state the following: He was not killed by any member of the armed forces that was subordinated to General Hadzihasanovic; and secondly, in relation to that particular event, there is nothing to indicate that General Hadzihasanovic knew anything about it whatsoever. The Prosecutor claims that nothing was done, and that on top of that the order issued by the commander of the Supreme Command Rasim Delic was not obeyed to, that is to say, the order to protect the civilian population. In spite of that, evidence obtained in the course of this trial it indicates quite clearly that straight away military police battalion visited Bugojno to check things out and to possibly provide assistance in case units stationed at Bugojno needed any assistance. There is a document from the command of the Operational Group Zapad to the commander of the 3rd Corps indicating that they did not need any assistance. Immediately upon receiving the orders from the Supreme Command, the chief of security went to Bugojno and together with the chief of security of the Operational Group Zapad. He visited all areas inhabited by the Croat population and issued special orders about strict compliance with the Geneva Convention, and there is no reason why he should think that the units would not obey those orders. When it first transpired that there was some mistreatment of prisoners, there was a special committee, Muratovic and Zlotrg testified to that. It was a Verification Mission. And they realised that prisoner Havranek was beaten to death, and the perpetrators were arrested and criminal proceedings were instituted against them. So this is all that a commander needs. His order as to how to treat prisoners can't rule out bad behaviour on the part of any of his subordinates. But his information was that on the one occasion that it did happen the measures were -- the relevant measures were implemented and individuals guilty of that crime were held accountable for their behaviour. Awhile ago I said that attention should be paid to the report of the ECMM and Rudy Gerritsen's testimony, and there is another problem. Bugojno was under the influenced of the civilian organs in Bugojno. According to the evidence we have, the communications were related to the communications of the civilian Presidency and the War Presidency. There's the decision of the Presidency to form the Iskra stadium. There is an order issued to the 307th Brigade that confirms that the events in Bugojno took place under the effective control to a large extent of the organs in Bugojno. With regard to the evidence and the analysis of the evidence, the Chamber will take into consideration all the facts that I have mentioned. The Defence believes that prisoners of war in Bugojno were inhumanely treated. Defence also believes that the corps commander previously took measures to prevent such acts. He did so by issuing orders on respecting the Geneva Conventions and by sending members of the command to implement these orders in the field. After he had discovered about certain events, he -- the commander took certain measures and found out that repressive measures were being taken against individuals who had committed these acts. And in the case of the gimnazija, for these reasons we believe that the commander should be acquitted because the gimnazija was not under the ABiH. As far as other events are concerned, the necessary and adequate measures were taken for events that he was aware of, and individuals who perpetrated these crimes were arrested and prosecuted. The commander had no knowledge of other events. And it is for these reasons that we believe that he should be acquitted on this count of the indictment. Mr. President, as you suggested, we believe that it is now time to adjourn. Tomorrow we'll have another 20 minutes, or half an hour perhaps, and we will conclude our presentation during that time.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll calculate the time that you still have, and I'll tell you how much time you have tomorrow officially. As the Prosecution had six hours, you should have the same number of hours. Thank you. It's quarter to two, and I invite you to return for the hearing that will start tomorrow at 9.00.
